55.title: Why Cats' Eyes Glow in the Dark #cats #science
55.description:
Shine a light at a cat in the dark and its eyes blaze green or gold. Yours don't. Cat eyes don't make any light: they bounce your light back. Right behind the retina, cats have a mirror-like layer called the tapetum lucidum. Light that slips past the light-sensing cells hits this layer and is reflected back through the retina, so it gets a second chance to be detected. Some of that reflected light escapes the eye, straight back toward your torch or camera flash, and that is the glow (eyeshine). It is part of why a cat can see with roughly a sixth of the light a person needs. The price: the reflected light scatters a little, so a cat's picture of the world is slightly blurrier than ours. Humans have no tapetum; the red-eye in flash photos is a much weaker reflection from the blood-rich layer at the back of the eye.

More: Why don't you see the hole in your vision? (long) https://youtu.be/i4d-ZYG2Ttc

56.title: Why Pen Caps Have a Hole #design #science
56.description:
Hold a pen cap up to the light and you can see a tiny hole at the tip. It is not there for the ink. Children chew pen caps, and now and then one gets breathed in and lodges in the windpipe. The hole lets some air keep flowing past the cap until a doctor can take it out. The safety standard ISO 11540 asks caps on pens likely to be used by children (up to 14) to let at least 8 litres of air a minute through, at a small pressure difference, or to be too big to breathe in at all (they must not pass through a 16 mm test ring). So the hole is a breathing hole, not a factory mistake.

More: Why plane windows have no corners https://youtube.com/shorts/ly6j5FGA5nI

57.title: Why a Wooden Spoon Stops a Pot Boiling Over #science #kitchen
57.description:
Lay a wooden spoon across a pot of pasta that is about to boil over, and the foam backs off. The spoon is not pressing it down. Starch from the pasta coats every bubble in a sticky skin, so the bubbles last and stack up into a foam that climbs out of the pot. A dry wooden spoon is cooler than the foam (wood carries heat away poorly) and porous, so a bubble that touches it bursts, and a burst bubble takes its neighbours with it.

The catch: it only buys you a little time. Once the spoon is as hot as the pot and soaked through, it stops bursting bubbles and the foam climbs right over. A bigger pot and lower heat work better, and stirring works too. Wood tends to work longer than a metal spoon, which heats up and wets through faster.

58.title: Why the First Second on a Clock Lasts Too Long #brain #illusion
58.description:
Stare at the dot, then jump your eyes to the clock: the second hand can seem to hang for a moment before it ticks again. The video didn't lag. This is the stopped-clock illusion (chronostasis). While your eyes jump (a saccade), your brain switches off the blurry view. Then it fills that gap with the clock, as if you had been looking at it all along, so the borrowed time is added to the first tick. It can feel up to about half a second longer. Bigger eye jumps give a bigger effect, so try it on a real wall clock across the room. And you do this all day: your eyes jump about three times a second.

59.title: How a Falling Cat Flips With Nothing to Push On #cats #science
59.description:
A cat falling upside down has nothing to push against, yet it lands on its feet. When Étienne-Jules Marey photographed a falling cat in 1894, the cat started with no spin, and some scientists suspected it had cheated by pushing off the hand that let it go. It had not. A rigid object could not do this, but a cat is not rigid: it bends in the middle, so its front and back halves can turn about different axes. With the front legs tucked in, the front half turns a long way while the stretched-out back half turns back only a little; then it swaps, and the back half catches up. Feet down. From very low (under about 30 to 60 cm) there is not enough time to complete the turn. Kittens develop this righting reflex at about 3 to 4 weeks and have it perfected by about 6 to 9 weeks.

More: Why do cats' eyes glow in the dark?

60.title: Why Ice Cream Gives You Brain Freeze (and the Tongue Fix) #science #body
60.description:
The ice cream is in your mouth, so why does your forehead hurt? Your brain is not freezing. The cold hits the roof of your mouth, and the blood vessels there tighten, then widen again fast. That change is picked up by the trigeminal nerve, which also serves your forehead, so your brain places the pain in the wrong spot (referred pain).

Speed matters: in one randomised trial with 145 pupils, eating ice cream in under 5 seconds gave 27% of them a headache, against 13% for those who took more than 30 seconds.

The fix doctors suggest: press your tongue (or thumb) against the roof of your mouth to warm it back up, or sip something warm. Brain freeze usually passes within seconds to a couple of minutes.
